In this exercise you will practise building a `ggplot2` plot one layer at a time.

By the end, you should be able to:

- identify the data, aesthetic mappings, and geometry in a plot,
- add one layer at a time using `+`,
- compare different geometries for showing the same variables,
- knit the completed document to HTML.

## Load packages and data

Load the `tidyverse` package. This includes `ggplot2` for plotting and `read_csv()` for loading data.

```{r}
# Load tidyverse.
library(tidyverse)
```

We will use data from @blomkvist2017reference.

The data file is in the `data` folder inside this weekly folder. Keep the `data` folder and this `.Rmd` file together, and the path below should work when you run chunks or knit the document.

If the following code returns `Error: 'data/blomkvist.csv' does not exist in current working directory`, check that you are working from the extracted weekly folder and that the `data` folder has not been moved.

```{r}
# Load the data.
d_blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")

# Remove rows where smoker status is missing.
d_blomkvist <- drop_na(d_blomkvist, smoker)
```

Start by inspecting the variables in the data frame.

```{r}
# Inspect the data frame.
glimpse(___)
```

## Data and aesthetics

A `ggplot()` call needs data. Most plots also need aesthetic mappings inside `aes()`.

In the code below:

- add `d_blomkvist` to `data =`,
- map dominant-foot reaction time to `x`,
- map non-dominant-foot reaction time to `y`.

```{r}
# Complete the data and aesthetic mappings.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___))
```

When you run the completed code, you should see a blank plot. This is expected: you have told R what data and mappings to use, but not what to draw yet.

## Add a geometry

A geometry tells `ggplot2` what visual marks to draw. Geometry functions usually start with `geom_`.

Add `geom_point()` to show each observation as a point.

```{r}
# Add points to the plot.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  ___
```

## Add a statistical summary

The same data and mappings can also be summarised. `stat_smooth()` adds a trend line that summarises the relationship between two variables.

Add `stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)` to show a straight-line trend.

```{r}
# Add a linear trend line.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  ___
```

## Combine layers

You can add more than one layer to the same plot.

Add both `geom_point()` and `stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)`.

```{r}
# Combine points and a trend line.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  ___ +
  ___
```

Now add `geom_rug()` as a third layer. Rug marks show the marginal distribution on each axis.

```{r}
# Add rug marks as another layer.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  ___ +
  ___ +
  ___
```

## Use a geometry for one variable

So far we have plotted two variables. Some geometries are used for one variable.

Create a histogram of `age` using `geom_histogram()`.

```{r}
# Plot the distribution of age.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___)) +
  ___
```

You may see a message like this: `stat_bin() using bins = 30`. This means that `ggplot2` chose 30 bins for the histogram.

Try setting the number of bins yourself. First try `bins = 5`, then try `bins = 50`.

```{r}
# Try different numbers of bins.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = ___)
```

Instead of the number of bins, you can set the width of each bin. For example, `binwidth = 5` means each bar spans 5 years of age.

```{r}
# Try a fixed bin width.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = ___)
```

## Another geometry for one variable

A density plot is another way to show the distribution of one continuous variable.

Change the previous plot to use `geom_density()`.

```{r}
# Show the distribution of age as a density plot.
ggplot(data = ___, mapping = aes(x = ___)) +
  ___
```

Look back at one of your completed plots and answer these questions.

1. Which data frame does the plot use?
2. Which variables are mapped inside `aes()`?
